mcqs.question: A page table entry has its valid bit set to invalid. What does the MMU do?
options: It always delivers SIGSEGV immediately
It silently returns zero for the access
It traps to the OS — the hardware itself doesn't know whether this means 'not loaded yet' or 'genuinely invalid access'
It automatically loads the page from swap without OS involvement
mcqs.explanation: The hardware only knows the entry is invalid and traps; distinguishing 'not yet loaded' from 'never valid' from 'swapped out' is entirely the OS fault handler's job using other bookkeeping. It doesn't auto-deliver SIGSEGV, doesn't silently return zero, and doesn't load from swap without the OS.

mcqs.question: How does a routine page fault differ from a true SIGSEGV-causing invalid access?
options: There's no real difference — both terminate the process
A page fault only happens during process startup, never afterward
A page fault is recoverable — the OS fixes it up and the faulting instruction re-executes successfully; a genuinely invalid access is what actually results in SIGSEGV
SIGSEGV happens first, then triggers a page fault afterward
mcqs.explanation: A routine page fault is recoverable and the instruction retries successfully; SIGSEGV is reserved for genuinely invalid accesses. It isn't limited to startup, doesn't always terminate the process, and SIGSEGV doesn't precede or trigger a fault.

mcqs.question: Memory access = 100 ns, page fault service time = 8 ms. At a fault rate of 0.001, what is roughly the effective access time?
options: About 100 ns, unaffected by the fault rate
About 8,100 ns
About 8 ms exactly
About 900 ns
mcqs.explanation: EAT = 0.999(100) + 0.001(8,000,000) ≈ 99.9 + 8,000 ≈ 8,100 ns. It's far from unaffected, well below the full 8 ms (since faults are rare), and not simply 900 ns.

mcqs.question: Immediately after fork(), why are both parent and child processes' pages marked read-only, even pages that were writable before the fork?
options: To permanently prevent either process from ever writing to memory
Because fork() itself is defined to only support read-only processes
So that any write attempt faults, letting the OS make a private copy of just that one page on demand instead of copying everything up front
To force the child process to always call exec() immediately
mcqs.explanation: Marking pages read-only after fork is what makes the write fault trigger a targeted, on-demand private copy — the essence of copy-on-write. It's not a permanent restriction, isn't a limitation of fork() itself, and doesn't force an immediate exec().

mcqs.question: A system's page fault rate rises from 0.01% to 1%. Why can this cause a severe latency regression rather than a proportionally small one?
options: Because fault handling time doesn't scale with rate at all
Because a 1% fault rate always exceeds the disk's total bandwidth
This can't happen — a 1% fault rate is negligible by definition
Because page faults cost orders of magnitude more than a normal memory access, so even a small rate increase dominates the weighted average access time
mcqs.explanation: Because a fault costs millions of times more than a normal access, even a rate that sounds small dominates the weighted effective-access-time formula — the disparity in cost, not the rate itself, is what matters. It isn't about disk bandwidth limits, and a 1% rate is not inherently negligible given this cost gap.

mcqs.question: What triggers the Linux OOM killer to terminate a process?
options: A process exceeding a fixed CPU time limit
Physical memory and swap space both being nearly exhausted, leaving a page fault with no way to be serviced
A process explicitly requesting to be terminated
Any single allocation request larger than 1 GB
mcqs.explanation: The OOM killer is a last resort for when there's genuinely no memory or swap left to service a fault, not a CPU-time or allocation-size rule, and it isn't a voluntary process request.
